intro: From metropolitan Denver to Colorado Springs and the state's mountain communities, buying a Colorado home involves expenses beyond the advertised purchase price.

Our free Colorado mortgage calculator helps you estimate monthly mortgage payments, property taxes, homeowners insurance and other recurring housing costs. Adjust your down payment, interest rate and loan term to compare properties and establish a homebuying budget that reflects your financial circumstances.

sections.heading: Quick Answer: How Much Is a Mortgage Payment in Colorado?

blocks.markdown:
A $540,000 home purchased with a 20% down payment and a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage at 6% would have a monthly principal and interest payment of approximately $2,590.06.

These figures assume no private mortgage insurance. The taxes, interest rate, insurance and association fees are illustrative rather than verified statewide averages.

Colorado's housing market covers large metropolitan areas, growing suburban communities, agricultural regions and mountain destinations.

The [US Census Bureau's Colorado housing statistics](https://www.census.gov/quickfacts/fact/table/CO/HSG495224) show that the median value of owner-occupied homes was $539,400 during the 2020–2024 survey period.

Median selected monthly ownership costs for homeowners with mortgages were $2,326, while the owner-occupied housing rate was 66.2%.

These historical figures provide a general picture of housing affordability, but they should not replace recent neighborhood-level property research.

Homes in Boulder or popular mountain destinations can have different prices and ownership costs from properties in Pueblo or smaller communities on the Eastern Plains.

Compare similar properties in your intended area and use realistic purchase prices when completing the calculator.

sections.heading: How to Use the Colorado Mortgage Calculator

blocks.markdown:
Enter the purchase price of the home you are considering. Add your expected down payment in dollars or as a percentage of the property's price.

Choose a repayment period and enter the annual mortgage interest rate offered by your lender.

For a more accurate estimate, enter annual property taxes, homeowners insurance premiums and monthly association fees.

If your conventional mortgage requires private mortgage insurance, include that expense as well.

Review your estimated monthly payment and the amortization schedule. Changing your down payment or interest rate allows you to compare the financial effects of different borrowing arrangements.

Use our national Mortgage Calculator if you are also considering properties outside Colorado.

sections.heading: How Colorado Property Taxes Are Calculated

blocks.markdown:
Colorado property taxes are imposed by local taxing authorities rather than through a uniform statewide property tax.

The amount you owe depends on the property's actual value, applicable statutory adjustments, assessment rates and local mill levies.

According to the [Colorado General Assembly's property tax overview](https://content.leg.colorado.gov/publications/property-taxes-colorado), property taxation supports local government services and school districts.

Importantly, Colorado introduced separate residential assessment rates for school district taxes and other local government taxes beginning with the 2025 tax year.

### Colorado residential assessment rates for 2026

The [Boulder County Assessor's property tax calculation guide](https://bouldercounty.gov/property-and-land/assessor/assessment/tax-calculation/) lists the following residential assessment rates for tax year 2026, generally payable in 2027:

- School district assessment rate: 7.05%.
- Other local government assessment rate: 6.8%.
- Local government value adjustment: 10% of the first $700,000 of actual property value.

These are assessment rates, not effective tax rates applied directly to your purchase price.

### Colorado property tax calculation example

Consider a residential property with an assessor-determined actual value of $540,000.

Assume a school district levy of 30 mills and a combined other local government levy of 50 mills. These levies are hypothetical.

The combined estimated annual tax would be $2,794.50, or approximately $232.88 per month.

Actual taxes can differ because of local levies, exemptions and other applicable rules. Consult your county assessor before relying on this calculation.

The [Colorado Property Tax Map](https://gis.colorado.gov/proptaxmap/) provides additional resources for investigating local taxation.

Homebuyers considering newer residential developments should investigate whether a property belongs to a metropolitan district.

These districts can finance roads, utilities and other public infrastructure. Their obligations may contribute additional mill levies to the property's annual tax bill.

Two homes with comparable purchase prices may therefore have different property tax expenses.

Ask the seller or developer for information about applicable district charges and outstanding financial obligations. Review the property's complete tax assessment rather than assuming that all developments in the same city have similar tax rates.

Do not count a metropolitan district levy twice if it is already included in your annual property tax estimate.

Colorado homeowners face different insurance risks depending on their property's location.

Homes along the Front Range and Eastern Plains may experience hailstorms, while properties near forests and mountain communities can face wildfire exposure.

The [Colorado Division of Insurance's wildfire consumer advisory](https://content.govdelivery.com/accounts/CODORA/bulletins/41f4de2) provides information about homeowner protections and coverage.

Obtain insurance quotes that account for the property's actual construction, roof condition, replacement cost and environmental exposure.

### Wind and hail deductibles

Some policies use percentage-based deductibles for wind or hail damage.

For example, a 2% deductible calculated against a $500,000 dwelling coverage limit would represent $10,000 in potential out-of-pocket costs for a covered claim to which that deductible applies.

Ask your insurer how each deductible works before selecting coverage.

### Insurance for mountain properties

A mountain home may have different rebuilding requirements, emergency access considerations and wildfire risks from an urban property.

Ask insurers about coverage availability and any conditions relating to property maintenance or wildfire mitigation.

Review exclusions carefully and investigate flood risk through the [FEMA Flood Map Service Center](https://msc.fema.gov/portal/home).
The following examples assume a 20% down payment, a 6% fixed interest rate and a 30-year repayment period.

These payments exclude taxes, insurance and association fees.

Add property-specific expenses using the calculator before comparing affordability.

The Colorado Housing and Finance Authority, commonly known as CHFA, offers mortgage programs and assistance through participating lenders.

### CHFA down payment assistance grant

The [CHFA down payment assistance program](https://www.chfainfo.com/homeownership/down-payment-assistance) offers an eligible grant of up to 3% of the first mortgage amount, capped at $25,000.

The grant does not require repayment, although the associated mortgage may carry a higher interest rate.

### CHFA second mortgage assistance

CHFA also offers deferred second mortgage assistance of up to 4% of the first mortgage amount, subject to a $25,000 cap and applicable program conditions.

Repayment becomes due when qualifying events occur, such as selling, refinancing or paying off the first mortgage.

Certain specialized programs offer different assistance arrangements.

Compare the complete financing costs rather than selecting a program solely because it offers a larger upfront contribution.

sections.heading: Additional Costs of Owning a Colorado Home

blocks.markdown:
Mountain properties may require spending on snow removal, heating, private road maintenance or specialized repairs.

Urban condominiums may have substantial association dues covering shared facilities and building insurance.

Ask for historical utility bills and association financial statements before purchasing. Review potential special assessments that might create unexpected expenses after closing.

sections.heading: How Much House Can You Afford in Colorado?

blocks.markdown:
Start with reliable monthly take-home income and account for transportation, groceries, childcare, insurance, savings and existing debts.

Our [Colorado Paycheck Calculator](/calculators/colorado-paycheck-calculator/) can help estimate your after-tax income. Use the [Debt to Income Ratio Calculator](/debt/debt-to-income-ratio-calculator/) to compare your financial obligations with gross monthly earnings.

Review the [CFPB's homebuying guidance](https://www.consumerfinance.gov/owning-a-home/) before selecting a lender or establishing your maximum purchase price.

### How much is a mortgage payment on a $540,000 Colorado home?

With a 20% down payment, 6% fixed interest and a 30-year term, monthly principal and interest would be approximately $2,590.06. Taxes, insurance and applicable fees increase total housing expenses.

### How are Colorado residential property taxes calculated?

Colorado uses property values, applicable value adjustments, assessment rates and local mill levies. Since 2025, separate residential assessment rates apply to school districts and other local governments.

### Can Colorado buyers receive down payment assistance?

Yes. CHFA offers eligible borrowers grants and deferred second mortgages. Assistance amounts, interest rates and qualifying requirements depend on the specific financing program.

Use our Colorado mortgage calculator to compare financing arrangements before making an offer. Include local taxes, insurance and other ownership costs to determine whether a property fits your overall financial plan.
